utterances.text: Great. So thank you very much. We're here tonight to review our single family existing buildings reach code proposal. And I know we have a big agenda, so I'll get right into it. State codes more and more are driven by the state's goals of 100% renewable energy and trying to get buildings to net zero, so there's no emissions from the buildings at all. And then locally, it's driven by our climate action Plan and general plan programs. The climate Action Plan was integrated into the general plan. And as you know, I like to say, have you ever reduced anything in your life by 40%? So we have to be able to attack it from every opportunity that we can. And buildings is one of the main areas for emissions. And then the county role, the county provides a lot of support. They lead the model reach code process every few years. They actually have adopted the reach code that we're bringing forward to you tonight. They support all the jurisdictions with community engagement and development of interfacing with the state and data and all sorts of stuff. And then on occasion, we call together an ad hoc subcommittee and council members Bushy and Yorin Scolati have helped us with some of the challenging questions as we went through this analysis. So why are we getting at buildings? So this is our emissions pie for San Rafael. This is our in boundary emissions, the Things that we actually create right here. This doesn't take into account the upstream emissions that are from the things that we purchase. But as you can see, the built environment, electricity and natural gas make up about 31% of our greenhouse gas emissions as of 2022. And the vast majority of it is natural gas, as more of our electricity gets to be more renewable. So again, in terms of the building and energy codes are updated on a three year code cycle. But then halfway through, they surprise us with these intervening codes. And generally they're very light, they're minor tweaks, but this year they're actually fairly substantial. And so part of our recommendation this year is to integrate some of those intervening codes into our local code. As Don got that award for making things simpler for people, this is that whole piece of it. Again, do you want to go looking two places for codes or can we integrate whenever possible so it's easier for applicants and for staff as well? And then every three years, we have this opportunity for reach codes. And the state supports reach codes. They want local jurisdictions to do reach codes. They support it by providing cost effectiveness studies. They provide it by providing data and helping you write the codes as well. The whole point is that a lot of these reach codes end up becoming state code later on. And they recognize this is a good way for local jurisdictions to get at their climate goals. So San Rafael typically enacts reach codes. We did the last cycle, we did the cycle before. And I'll go over a little bit of the reach codes that you all adopted at the end of 2022 as well. So there was two main things. One was existing new construction, and it was an electrification requirement. We prohibited natural gas in new construction for most building types, including residential and commercial and multifamily. And then we prohibited, if you went and you built a new building, you couldn't go and add gas later. There were many exceptions, including restaurants and for things like infeasibility or hardship. And then we also included a prohibition on gas line extensions in existing single family homes. And that whole idea was what gas you have is the gas that you get. If you wanted to increase your gas use by putting in a hot tub, for instance, you had to decrease it someplace else. And then effective was January 4, 2023. The other part of that reach code was this robust electric vehicle reach code. And this is getting that chicken egg piece about. Do, do you need to have the electric vehicle charging infrastructure first? Do you get the vehicle first? Well, what if I live in an apartment complex? And so this Reach code actually came from a lot of work in the South Bay at Peninsula Clean Energy. And we looked at that in the county and we adopted it together. And the idea there was let's get a lot of EV readiness in multifamily. If you get it in there and you get it right up to the stub out, all you need to do is pop in a charger later. It's much easier than having to pull conduit or do a lot of electrical upgrades later. So that was the essential piece for electric field requirements. Since then, of course, there was the California Restaurant association case versus the City of Berkeley. City of Berkeley was the first in the state to adopt an all electric ordinance and prohibited gas for new construction. And the CRA sued and actually lost initially. But then it went to the ninth Circuit Court of Appeal which agreed that based on federal law, the the appeals court and Genevieve can correct me if I'm wrong, basically said the Energy Policy and Conservation act gave the federal authorities the only authority to regulate covered appliances and the energy that goes to them. So any kind of appliance, so regulating it and saying no gas was basically stepping on the feet of the federal government to be able to regulate energy efficiency in these covered appliances. It doesn't affect the building envelope. It doesn't affect things like the insulation and windows and those types of things. It affects these covered products. So in essence, Berkeley Lawson has to repeal their ordinance and it affects all cities with gas bans, including Summerfield.
